title: Calm, quiet, peaceful lessons 29, 2026
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer begins from a list of large problems in English education, including falling attendance, rising mental health concerns and persistent disadvantage gaps, and argues that schools should start with the one lever they control: better teaching in every classroom. He proposes that the uncontroversial core of better teaching is classrooms that are calm, quiet and peaceful, and he points to a video of an ordinary school with an average intake as proof that this is achievable. He cites survey data showing that majorities of primary and secondary teachers accept low-level disruption as inevitable, and he flatly calls that belief wrong. Behaviour, he argues, is the precondition for every other initiative, from curriculum to belonging policies, because teachers cannot teach and students cannot learn amid constant disruption. His prescription is centralised, consistent behaviour policies, training in concrete routines such as FLMOP, and national support for behaviour and wider social infrastructure. The post ends with a note that Carousel Teaching sells this kind of support.
points: Boxer reframes system-wide school improvement as a modest, unglamorous goal: better teaching in every classroom, beginning with calm, quiet and peaceful lessons.
He challenges the common acceptance of low-level disruption, citing that 54 percent of primary and 40 percent of secondary teachers think staff must tolerate some.
The featured school is deliberately ordinary, with average free-school-meal numbers and above-average EHCPs, which shows that calm classrooms result from school actions rather than special intake.
Behaviour is positioned as a precondition: no curriculum, oracy strategy or belonging policy can compensate if lessons are routinely disrupted.
The remedy is centralised, transparent, consistent policy plus training in precise routines such as FLMOP, supported by national investment in behaviour capacity.
quotes: There aren’t many people who would disagree with that. It feels pretty obvious, and it also feels necessary in that if classrooms aren’t calm, quiet and peaceful, it’s unlikely that we will get to the point of “better teaching in every classroom.

Disruption is in fact so commonplace that teachers have just accepted it as normal and to be expected - 54% of primary teachers and 40% of secondary teachers agree that “staff inevitably must tolerate some low-level disruptions”.
Teachers who believe that they should inevitably tolerate some low-level disruptions are wrong.

It’s not a startup. It doesn’t rely on zero tolerance, silent corridors, or line-ups before every lesson. It has an average number of students on free school meals and an above-average number of students with EHCPs.

It doesn’t really matter if you have an amazing curriculum, Teaching and Learning playbook, restorative approach, oracy strategy or “belonging” policy: if students are calling out, answering back, chatting and disrupting lessons, teachers cannot teach and students cannot learn.

To achieve this, schools would need to create behaviour policies that are centralised, robust, transparent and consistent. They would need to train their teachers in the implementation of precise, concrete routines and simple, consistent systems.
While most of the variables exist outside of the school gates, there are things we can control, and things we know work, because other schools just like ours have tried them, and they’ve worked.
